perspective:
From Carolyn Abebe’s perspective:

- I am Carolyn Abebe, a bank teller at a community bank. Marilyn Olson is a colleague/sales representative I have recently started working with.
- During a busy week at the bank, I noticed Marilyn was unusually quiet and withdrawn, unlike her normally engaging demeanor.
- I asked Marilyn if everything was alright. She said she was overwhelmed with work and some personal stuff, and thanked me for asking.
- Later, Marilyn responded curtly to me in another interaction. I felt confused and slightly hurt.
- I told Marilyn I hoped I hadn’t overstepped, that I’ve had tough times too, and that talking can sometimes help. She said she appreciated it, apologized if she seemed off, and said it had been a hard week.
- After that, I felt relieved and hopeful because Marilyn seemed to respond positively.
- I invited Marilyn to a small weekend get-together with friends. She said it sounded lovely, thanked me, and said she’d love to join.
- Even after friendly interactions outside work, I perceived Marilyn as still maintaining a professional distance at the bank. I felt disappointed.
- I asked Marilyn if we could talk about our work dynamic and told her I felt an unexplained distance between us. She said she hadn’t realized that, apologized if it seemed that way, and agreed to talk about improving collaboration.
- After our private meeting, I believed we had cleared the air and better understood each other’s professional expectations and personal boundaries. I felt content and optimistic.
- I proposed teaming up on the new project proposal. Marilyn said that was a great idea, was glad we had talked, and looked forward to working more closely with me.

I only have access to Marilyn’s outward behavior and what she explicitly told me in these interactions; I do not know her private reasons or feelings beyond that.
